articles.title: Editor's Notes
articles.summary: This Editor's Notes update includes the installation of a portable toilet at the Henry Coe State Park observing area, and details the upcoming Orionid meteor shower, peaking October 21/22, which originates from Halley's Comet. It also recounts Bill Arnett's Lick Tour experience, particularly highlighting the 120-inch telescope. The article concludes with a comprehensive schedule of star parties, general meetings, and a beginning astronomy class for October and November.

articles.title: Good Luck Near Yosemite John Gleason
articles.summary: John Gleason details a highly successful astrophotography trip near Yosemite in late August, where he experienced exceptionally calm and transparent observing conditions. These rare conditions, free from atmospheric turbulence and wind, allowed for incredibly detailed, high-contrast, and color-saturated images of the Pelican Nebula and M13. The ST-4 autoguider's 0/0 readouts further confirmed the unusual stability of the night.

articles.title: Editor, from p. 1
articles.summary: This article shares various updates including an observer's positive experience with a 36-inch refractor for double stars, noting its exceptional clarity. It also provides brief community news, mentioning a board member's minor accident at an observing site and a long-time observer's quick recovery from a heart attack. Finally, it reminds astronomers to pay park fees at observing locations to support these valuable facilities.

articles.title: Yosemite from p. 1
articles.summary: The author recounts a long night of astronomical observation and astrophotography using an Astro Physics 7" F/7 refractor. The session included detailed visual observations of Jupiter, the Pleiades, M31, M33, and Saturn, along with views of the Pelican/North American Nebula and capturing astrophotographs. The observer also witnessed a bolide meteor and zodiacal light, highlighting improved sky transparency and the joys of the hobby despite minor equipment issues.

articles.title: Bill Arnett
articles.summary: The article advocates for a more aggressive and risk-tolerant approach to U.S. space exploration, specifically urging human missions to Mars. The author criticizes NASA's current timidity, asserting that taking dangerous risks, reminiscent of the Apollo era, is crucial not just for scientific advancement but to rekindle America's pioneering spirit. He argues that this grand, challenging goal is essential to overcome cultural malaise, provide societal inspiration, and is more vital than perceived terrestrial problems or cautious, robot-centric exploration.

articles.title: ASTRO ADS
articles.summary: This document features a section called "ASTRO ADS" with classified listings for used astronomical equipment, including a TeleVue Panoptic eyepiece, an 8" Mylar Solar Filter, and a Meade LX-200 telescope. It also provides guidelines for submitting free non-commercial ads to the Editor, specifying contact methods and ad duration.

articles.title: The Shallow Sky
articles.summary: This article provides an observing guide for October, highlighting excellent planetary viewing opportunities, particularly for Saturn and Jupiter. Jupiter offers active cloud bands and interesting moon phenomena, while Saturn's rings are more open this year. Lunar observing is presented as more challenging, with best views of the Third Quarter Moon in the early morning and limited libration opportunities, though a close approach between Saturn and the Moon is noted for early risers.

articles.title: Freeman On Everything
articles.summary: Jay Freeman's "Freeman On Everything", an updated piece from "Notes For Beginners", discusses the various types of telescopes that amateur astronomers can purchase. The article serves as a guide for those looking to buy their first or next telescope.

articles.title: High-Tech Conversation-Stopper:
articles.summary: The article humorously describes the "High-Tech Conversation-Stopper" — typically an expensive apochromatic refractor — used to 'shame' owners of large, homemade Dobsonians. The author suggests using technical jargon like diffraction rings and modulation transfer functions to assert superiority, noting that while their own 90mm Vixen fluorite refractor isn't as impressive, it serves this purpose by virtue of its sophistication and cost.

articles.title: On Venus:
articles.summary: The author recounts a surprising naked-eye observation of Venus in daylight on August 31, 1997, about an hour before sunset. Despite the sun's glare, Venus was clearly visible, even with sunglasses, an observation aided by thin clouds. The experience of seeing Venus so obviously in full daylight was described as startling and impressive.

articles.title: On Telrads:
articles.summary: The author expresses a strong preference for a straight-through, magnifying finder (30-40mm aperture) over unit-magnification finders like the Telrad for their telescopes. This preference is based on their ability to use a straight-through finder as a reflex sight, the necessity of magnification for accurately locating faint objects using atlas stars, and the particular advantages for observing double stars by minimizing eyepiece changes. The article also includes a brief, unrelated anecdote from Lick Observatory.

articles.title: Don Machholz
articles.summary: The article reports on recent comet discoveries, including C/1997 P2 (Spacewatch) and six new comets found by the SOHO satellite, bringing its total to 26. It also notes the current visibility of Comets Hale-Bopp and Meunier-Dupouy. Additionally, it provides guidance for amateur astronomers interested in hunting for faint Kreutz Sungrazing comets in the morning sky, suggesting CCD imaging for fainter objects and visual methods for brighter, rarer finds.

articles.title: Ephemerides (for 0h UT)
articles.summary: This document provides ephemerides for comets C/1995 O1 (Hale-Bopp) and C/1997 J2 (Meunier-Dupouy) for the period of early October to early November, listing their predicted Right Ascension, Declination, Elongation, Sky visibility, and Visual Magnitude. It also includes detailed orbital elements for both comets, such as perihelion date and distance, inclination, and eccentricity.

articles.title: NOTES TO HELP YOU MAKE BETTER USE OF COMET COMMENTS
articles.summary: This article serves as a comprehensive guide for amateur astronomers on how to interpret and effectively utilize the information provided in "Comet Comments" by Don Machholz. It meticulously explains various data points crucial for comet observation, including ephemerides like position, predicted brightness, and sky visibility. Furthermore, it details the meaning of orbital elements, assisting readers in understanding comet trajectories for visual tracking and use with computer programs.

articles.title: CELESTIAL CALENDAR OCTOBER 1997
articles.summary: This document, titled 'Celestial Calendar October 1997' by Richard Stanton, serves as a brief guide for the month. It highlights that Daylight Savings Time concludes on October 26th, followed by the commencement of Pacific Standard Time on October 27th.

articles.title: Lunar
articles.summary: This document provides a table detailing the major lunar phases (New Moon, First Quarter, Full Moon, Last Quarter) for a specific month. For each phase, it lists the exact time and date (in PDT), along with the corresponding rise, transit, and set times of the Moon.

articles.title: Mercury
articles.summary: This document provides ephemeris data for the planet Mercury, including its magnitude and approximate distance from the Sun in astronomical units. It lists rise, transit, and set times, along with its celestial coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination) for three specific dates.

articles.title: Venus
articles.summary: This document presents an astronomical ephemeris for Venus, providing its rise, transit, and set times, along with its right ascension and declination for three specific dates. It also includes the planet's heliocentric distance (0.81 A.U.) and visual magnitude (-5.1), offering predictive data for observers.

articles.title: Mars
articles.summary: This document provides an astronomical ephemeris for Mars, detailing its celestial coordinates and visibility data for three specific dates (the 7th, 17th, and 27th) within a month. It lists the planet's rise, transit, and set times, along with its Right Ascension, Declination, apparent magnitude, and distance in Astronomical Units.

articles.title: Jupiter
articles.summary: This document provides an ephemeris for Jupiter, detailing its magnitude, distance, and specific rise, transit, and set times for various dates in a given period. It also includes the corresponding Right Ascension and Declination coordinates for Jupiter on those dates, aiding in its observation.

articles.title: Saturn
articles.summary: This document provides an ephemeris for Saturn, detailing its rise, transit, and set times, along with its right ascension and declination for three specific dates within a month. It also includes Saturn's average distance from Earth (8.39 A.U.) and its apparent magnitude (+0.6). This information is useful for observers planning to locate and view the planet.

articles.title: SOL Star Type G2V Intelligent Life in System?
articles.summary: This article presents a table of astronomical data, including 'Hours of Darkness,' rise, transit, and set times, along with celestial coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination). While the title provocatively references the Sun (SOL Star Type G2V) and intelligent life within its system, the core content consists of technical observational data, likely an ephemeris.

articles.title: Astronomical Twilight
articles.summary: This document presents a tabular listing of astronomical twilight start and end times. The data is organized by Julian Date, providing specific 'Begin' and 'End' times for several entries. It serves as a reference for predicting twilight periods on particular days.

articles.title: Siderealtime
articles.summary: This document presents a concise table illustrating the relationship between Transit Right Ascension at Local Midnight and the corresponding sidereal times on specific dates. It serves as a practical reference for understanding how sidereal time varies daily relative to celestial coordinates, crucial for astronomical calculations and observations.

articles.title: Darkest Saturday Night
articles.summary: This document outlines the astronomical conditions for the evening of October 4, 1997, highlighting the times for sunset, the end of astronomical twilight, and moonset. These details suggest an exceptionally dark night suitable for astronomical observation, as the moon sets relatively early after twilight ends.

articles.title: ACTIVITIES THROUGH OTHER CLUBS
articles.summary: The article announces that the TAC club holds regular midweek observing sessions every Wednesday at the Montebello site, located on Page Mill Road near Skyline. These events are highlighted as a congenial and convenient opportunity for astronomical observation.

articles.title: October
articles.summary: The document lists two astronomy events for October: a public night at Van Meter School on October 10th and a lunar observing session at Fremont Peak or Henry Coe on October 11th, both organized by TAC.

articles.title: November
articles.summary: This document outlines a schedule of astronomical events for November, including star parties hosted by HVAG at Grant Ranch and public observing nights by TAC at Van Meter School and Fremont Peak or Henry Coe for lunar observing. Additionally, it provides contact information for the SJAA hotline, web address, and mailing list subscription details.

articles.title: DIRECTIONS TO SJAA PLACES
articles.summary: This document provides detailed driving directions to three key locations used by the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA): Houge Park, Henry Coe State Park, and Fremont Peak State Park. Each entry includes specific turn-by-turn instructions from major highways, along with notes about fees or specific meeting spots within the parks.

articles.title: August Board Meeting
articles.summary: The August Board Meeting covered routine reports, noting a slight membership decline. A key action was approving a resolution to support renaming Fremont Peak State Park to Fremont Peak Astronomical Park, a community effort members are encouraged to join. The meeting also discussed improving communication via the SJAA mailing list and the desirability of reporting board minutes, while inviting members to participate in future meetings to strengthen the club.

articles.title: Officers and Board of Directors
articles.summary: This document lists the current officers and Board of Directors for an organization. It includes the names and phone numbers for key roles such as President, Vice President, Secretary, Treasurer, and several Directors.

articles.title: Ephemeris Staff
articles.summary: This document outlines the staff members for 'Ephemeris', detailing their respective roles and contact phone numbers. It lists the Editor, two Circulation contacts, and the Layout designer.

articles.title: Telescope Loaner Program Status
articles.summary: This document provides a status update for a telescope loaner program, detailing the current borrowers, due dates, and availability of various telescopes. Several telescopes are available for immediate loan, and there is currently no waiting list. SJAA members interested in borrowing equipment are encouraged to contact Mike Koop to reserve a scope.

articles.title: Submit
articles.summary: The San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) encourages its members to submit articles for publication in its monthly newsletter, the *SJAA Ephemeris*. Submissions, including the author's name and phone number, should be emailed to Dave North by the tenth of the month to be included in the following issue.

articles.title: San Jose Astronomical Association Membership Form
articles.summary: This document is a membership form for the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA), detailing options for new or renewal memberships, including standard and junior rates, and an optional Sky & Telescope subscription. It provides instructions for submitting the form and payment via check to the treasurer, along with contact information and mailing address for the organization.
